items.title: Modern Judaism has Orthodox, Conservative, Reform and Reconstructionist branches
items.claim: What distinguishes the main Jewish denominations?

options.text: There are no real denominational differences

Orthodox (Modern Orthodox, Haredi), Conservative (Masorti in UK), Reform, and Reconstructionist — distinguished mainly by their stance on the binding nature of Halakhah (Jewish law) and engagement with modernity

items.reveal:
Reform Judaism emerged in early 19th-century Germany (Israel Jacobson, Abraham Geiger), arguing for adapting tradition to modern reason. Modern Orthodox (Samson Raphael Hirsch) defended strict observance of Halakhah while engaging modern life. Haredi (often called 'ultra-Orthodox') resists much of modernity.

Conservative/Masorti Judaism (Zacharias Frankel, Solomon Schechter at JTS New York from 1902) is a middle path — Halakhah binding but historically developing. Reconstructionist Judaism (Mordecai Kaplan, 1922) sees Judaism as an evolving religious civilisation.

In Israel the Chief Rabbinate is Orthodox and controls marriage and conversion law; in the US, Reform is the largest denomination by membership.
items.why: Religions are internally diverse. Judaism's denominational landscape sets up the central modern question — how do tradition and modernity relate? — in structurally different ways.

items.title: Theravada and Mahayana are the two major Buddhist traditions
items.claim: How do Theravada and Mahayana differ?

options.text: Theravada ('teaching of the elders') dominant in Sri Lanka, Thailand, Myanmar, Cambodia, Laos — emphasises the Pali Canon and arhat ideal; Mahayana ('great vehicle') dominant in East Asia and Vietnam — emphasises bodhisattva path and Sanskrit/Chinese sutras; Tibetan Vajrayana is sometimes treated as a third stream

items.reveal:
The split developed in the centuries after the Buddha's death, with the Second Council (around 100 years after his parinirvana) marking early disagreements. Mahayana texts (Prajnaparamita Sutras, Lotus Sutra) emerged from around the 1st century BCE.

The bodhisattva ideal — postponing one's own final liberation to help all beings — is central to Mahayana. Theravada acknowledges bodhisattvas (including the historical Buddha before his enlightenment) but emphasises the arhat ideal.

Tibetan Buddhism is often treated as a separate Vajrayana branch. Zen and Pure Land are East Asian Mahayana developments.
items.why: Calling Buddhism 'one religion' obscures real diversity. The traditions share core teachings but differ on the path, the goal, the authoritative texts, and the role of devotion.

items.title: British religious affiliation has dropped sharply since the 1960s
items.claim: What does the 2021 UK Census show about religion?

options.text: For the first time, less than half of England and Wales (46.2%) identified as Christian; 37.2% had no religion; Islam grew to 6.5%; Hindu, Sikh, Jewish, Buddhist and Other religions made up the remainder
All religions are at the same percentage

items.reveal:
The 2001 Census recorded 72% Christian; 2011 recorded 59%; 2021 recorded 46% in England and Wales. The 'no religion' category rose from 15% (2001) to 25% (2011) to 37% (2021). Scotland (2022 census) showed similar trends; Northern Ireland remains more religious.

Muslim population: 3% (2001), 5% (2011), 6.5% (2021).

Secularisation theory (Bryan Wilson, Peter Berger) predicted declining religious influence with modernity. The reality has been more complex — declining institutional affiliation alongside persistent or growing 'spiritual but not religious' identification and increasing pluralism.
items.why: British religion is restructured, not just declining. The Census numbers show a more religiously plural country where institutional Christianity has lost its majority position — major implications for education, ethics and public life.
